43:36.ar: وَمَن يَعۡشُ عَن ذِكۡرِ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ نُقَيِّضۡ لَهُۥ شَيۡطَٰنࣰ ا فَهُوَ لَهُۥ قَرِينࣱ‏
43:36.en: And whoever is blinded from remembrance of the Most Merciful - We appoint for him a devil, and he is to him a companion

43:37.ar: وَإِنَّهُمۡ لَيَصُدُّونَهُمۡ عَنِ ٱلسَّبِيلِ وَيَحۡسَبُونَ أَنَّهُم مُّهۡتَدُونَ
43:37.en: And indeed, the devils avert them from the way [of guidance] while they think that they are [rightly] guided

43:38.ar: حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا جَآءَنَا قَالَ يَٰلَيۡتَ بَيۡنِي وَبَيۡنَكَ بُعۡدَ ٱلۡمَشۡرِقَيۡنِ فَبِئۡسَ ٱلۡقَرِينُ
43:38.en: Until, when he comes to Us [at Judgement], he says [to his companion], "Oh, I wish there was between me and you the distance between the east and west - how wretched a companion

43:39.ar: وَلَن يَنفَعَكُمُ ٱلۡيَوۡمَ إِذ ظَّلَمۡتُمۡ أَنَّكُمۡ فِي ٱلۡعَذَابِ مُشۡتَرِكُونَ
43:39.en: And never will it benefit you that Day, when you have wronged, that you are [all] sharing in the punishment

43:40.ar: أَفَأَنتَ تُسۡمِعُ ٱلصُّمَّ أَوۡ تَهۡدِي ٱلۡعُمۡيَ وَمَن كَانَ فِي ضَلَٰلࣲ مُّبِينࣲ‏
43:40.en: Then will you make the deaf hear, [O Muhammad], or guide the blind or he who is in clear error

43:41.ar: فَإِمَّا نَذۡهَبَنَّ بِكَ فَإِنَّا مِنۡهُم مُّنتَقِمُونَ
43:41.en: And whether [or not] We take you away [in death], indeed, We will take retribution upon them

43:42.ar: أَوۡ نُرِيَنَّكَ ٱلَّذِي وَعَدۡنَٰهُمۡ فَإِنَّا عَلَيۡهِم مُّقۡتَدِرُونَ
43:42.en: Or whether [or not] We show you that which We have promised them, indeed, We are Perfect in Ability

43:43.ar: فَٱسۡتَمۡسِكۡ بِٱلَّذِيٓ أُوحِيَ إِلَيۡكَۖ إِنَّكَ عَلَىٰ صِرَٰطࣲ مُّسۡتَقِيمࣲ‏
43:43.en: So adhere to that which is revealed to you. Indeed, you are on a straight path

43:44.ar: وَإِنَّهُۥ لَذِكۡرࣱ لَّكَ وَلِقَوۡمِكَۖ وَسَوۡفَ تُسۡـَٔلُونَ
43:44.en: And indeed, it is a remembrance for you and your people, and you [all] are going to be questioned

43:45.ar: وَسۡـَٔلۡ مَنۡ أَرۡسَلۡنَا مِن قَبۡلِكَ مِن رُّسُلِنَآ أَجَعَلۡنَا مِن دُونِ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ ءَالِهَةࣰ يُعۡبَدُونَ
43:45.en: And ask those We sent before you of Our messengers; have We made besides the Most Merciful deities to be worshipped

43:22.ar: بَلۡ قَالُوٓاْ إِنَّا وَجَدۡنَآ ءَابَآءَنَا عَلَىٰٓ أُمَّةࣲ وَإِنَّا عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَٰرِهِم مُّهۡتَدُونَ
43:22.en: Rather, they say, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and we are in their footsteps [rightly] guided

43:23.ar: وَكَذَٰلِكَ مَآ أَرۡسَلۡنَا مِن قَبۡلِكَ فِي قَرۡيَةࣲ مِّن نَّذِيرٍ إِلَّا قَالَ مُتۡرَفُوهَآ إِنَّا وَجَدۡنَآ ءَابَآءَنَا عَلَىٰٓ أُمَّةࣲ وَإِنَّا عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَٰرِهِم مُّقۡتَدُونَ
43:23.en: And similarly, We did not send before you any warner into a city except that its affluent said, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and we are, in their footsteps, following

43:24.ar: ۞قَٰلَ أَوَلَوۡ جِئۡتُكُم بِأَهۡدَىٰ مِمَّا وَجَدتُّمۡ عَلَيۡهِ ءَابَآءَكُمۡۖ قَالُوٓاْ إِنَّا بِمَآ أُرۡسِلۡتُم بِهِۦ كَٰفِرُونَ
43:24.en: [Each warner] said, "Even if I brought you better guidance than that [religion] upon which you found your fathers?" They said, "Indeed we, in that with which you were sent, are disbelievers

43:25.ar: فَٱنتَقَمۡنَا مِنۡهُمۡۖ فَٱنظُرۡ كَيۡفَ كَانَ عَٰقِبَةُ ٱلۡمُكَذِّبِينَ
43:25.en: So we took retribution from them; then see how was the end of the deniers

43:26.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ إِبۡرَٰهِيمُ لِأَبِيهِ وَقَوۡمِهِۦٓ إِنَّنِي بَرَآءࣱ مِّمَّا تَعۡبُدُونَ
43:26.en: And [mention, O Muhammad], when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am disassociated from that which you worship

43:27.en: Except for He who created me; and indeed, He will guide me

43:28.ar: وَجَعَلَهَا كَلِمَةَۢ بَاقِيَةࣰ فِي عَقِبِهِۦ لَعَلَّهُمۡ يَرۡجِعُونَ
43:28.en: And he made it a word remaining among his descendants that they might return [to it]

43:29.ar: بَلۡ مَتَّعۡتُ هَٰٓؤُلَآءِ وَءَابَآءَهُمۡ حَتَّىٰ جَآءَهُمُ ٱلۡحَقُّ وَرَسُولࣱ مُّبِينࣱ‏
43:29.en: However, I gave enjoyment to these [people of Makkah] and their fathers until there came to them the truth and a clear Messenger

43:30.ar: وَلَمَّا جَآءَهُمُ ٱلۡحَقُّ قَالُواْ هَٰذَا سِحۡرࣱ وَإِنَّا بِهِۦ كَٰفِرُونَ
43:30.en: But when the truth came to them, they said, "This is magic, and indeed we are, concerning it, disbelievers

43:31.ar: وَقَالُواْ لَوۡلَا نُزِّلَ هَٰذَا ٱلۡقُرۡءَانُ عَلَىٰ رَجُلࣲ مِّنَ ٱلۡقَرۡيَتَيۡنِ عَظِيمٍ
43:31.en: And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a great man from [one of] the two cities

43:32.ar: أَهُمۡ يَقۡسِمُونَ رَحۡمَتَ رَبِّكَۚ نَحۡنُ قَسَمۡنَا بَيۡنَهُم مَّعِيشَتَهُمۡ فِي ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَاۚ وَرَفَعۡنَا بَعۡضَهُمۡ فَوۡقَ بَعۡضࣲ دَرَجَٰتࣲ لِّيَتَّخِذَ بَعۡضُهُم بَعۡضࣰ ا سُخۡرِيࣰّ اۗ وَرَحۡمَتُ رَبِّكَ خَيۡرࣱ مِّمَّا يَجۡمَعُونَ
43:32.en: Do they distribute the mercy of your Lord? It is We who have apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world and have raised some of them above others in degrees [of rank] that they may make use of one another for service. But the mercy of your Lord is better than whatever they accumulate

43:33.ar: وَلَوۡلَآ أَن يَكُونَ ٱلنَّاسُ أُمَّةࣰ وَٰحِدَةࣰ لَّجَعَلۡنَا لِمَن يَكۡفُرُ بِٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ لِبُيُوتِهِمۡ سُقُفࣰ ا مِّن فِضَّةࣲ وَمَعَارِجَ عَلَيۡهَا يَظۡهَرُونَ
43:33.en: And if it were not that the people would become one community [of disbelievers], We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful - for their houses - ceilings and stairways of silver upon which to mount

43:34.ar: وَلِبُيُوتِهِمۡ أَبۡوَٰبࣰ ا وَسُرُرًا عَلَيۡهَا يَتَّكِـُٔونَ
43:34.en: And for their houses - doors and couches [of silver] upon which to recline

43:35.ar: وَزُخۡرُفࣰ اۚ وَإِن كُلُّ ذَٰلِكَ لَمَّا مَتَٰعُ ٱلۡحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنۡيَاۚ وَٱلۡأٓخِرَةُ عِندَ رَبِّكَ لِلۡمُتَّقِينَ
43:35.en: And gold ornament. But all that is not but the enjoyment of worldly life. And the Hereafter with your Lord is for the righteous

7:156.ar: ۞وَٱكۡتُبۡ لَنَا فِي هَٰذِهِ ٱلدُّنۡيَا حَسَنَةࣰ وَفِي ٱلۡأٓخِرَةِ إِنَّا هُدۡنَآ إِلَيۡكَۚ قَالَ عَذَابِيٓ أُصِيبُ بِهِۦ مَنۡ أَشَآءُۖ وَرَحۡمَتِي وَسِعَتۡ كُلَّ شَيۡءࣲۚ فَسَأَكۡتُبُهَا لِلَّذِينَ يَتَّقُونَ وَيُؤۡتُونَ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ وَٱلَّذِينَ هُم بِـَٔايَٰتِنَا يُؤۡمِنُونَ
7:156.en: And decree for us in this world [that which is] good and [also] in the Hereafter; indeed, we have turned back to You." [Allah] said, "My punishment - I afflict with it whom I will, but My mercy encompasses all things." So I will decree it [especially] for those who fear Me and give zakah and those who believe in Our verses

6:12.ar: قُل لِّمَن مَّا فِي ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضِۖ قُل لِّلَّهِۚ كَتَبَ عَلَىٰ نَفۡسِهِ ٱلرَّحۡمَةَۚ لَيَجۡمَعَنَّكُمۡ إِلَىٰ يَوۡمِ ٱلۡقِيَٰمَةِ لَا رَيۡبَ فِيهِۚ ٱلَّذِينَ خَسِرُوٓاْ أَنفُسَهُمۡ فَهُمۡ لَا يُؤۡمِنُونَ
6:12.en: Say, "To whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and earth?" Say, "To Allah." He has decreed upon Himself mercy. He will surely assemble you for the Day of Resurrection, about which there is no doubt. Those who will lose themselves [that Day] do not believe

4:76.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُواْ يُقَٰتِلُونَ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱللَّهِۖ وَٱلَّذِينَ كَفَرُواْ يُقَٰتِلُونَ فِي سَبِيلِ ٱلطَّٰغُوتِ فَقَٰتِلُوٓاْ أَوۡلِيَآءَ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنِۖ إِنَّ كَيۡدَ ٱلشَّيۡطَٰنِ كَانَ ضَعِيفًا
4:76.en: Those who believe fight in the cause of Allah, and those who disbelieve fight in the cause of Taghut. So fight against the allies of Satan. Indeed, the plot of Satan has ever been weak

AmI8Q6zR_S4.speaker_note: listed lecturer is Dr. Adnan Rajeh; weekend Fajr dars continuing his Az-Zukhruf series
AmI8Q6zR_S4.title: Fajr Dars: Az-Zukhruf, Verses 36-45
AmI8Q6zR_S4.one_line: Tafsir of Az-Zukhruf 43:36-45 on the materialist who cannot see the remembrance of al-Rahman, his devil companion, and holding fast whatever the outcome.
AmI8Q6zR_S4.summary: Continuing his reading of Az-Zukhruf, a surah he sees as a warning against a one-dimensional, materialistic view of the world, he explains verses 36 to 45. Zukhruf is what shines outside with no substance inside, and he warns that young people are growing up measuring success only by fame and wealth. The word for turning away from al-Rahman's remembrance describes someone who sees only what shines; such a person is never satisfied and becomes unable to hear spiritual truth. Allah assigns him a devil companion: either a jinn who simply opens a catalogue of temptations suited to his weakness, or, far worse, human companions. He rejects the idea that jinn take over a person and urges that people with psychosis be taken to mental health professionals, not exorcists, recounting a young man who nearly died after an exorcism. Those led astray think they are guided, which he applies to running masajid like businesses instead of as houses of service like the Prophet's masjid with Ahl al-Suffah. The verses then tell the Prophet he cannot make the deaf hear and may die before seeing success, so the true measure is holding fast to revelation on the straight path, for that is what everyone will be asked about.

outline.heading: Opening
Az-Zukhruf: a warning against one-dimensional materialism
outline.gist: The surah, among the Ha-Mim cluster of warnings to those who carry the message, takes on materialism from many angles and is especially relatable today.

outline.heading: Recap: idols, Ibrahim and judging the Prophet by wealth
outline.gist: Earlier verses showed idol worship and the oppression of women driven by profit, blind following of forefathers, Quraysh dismissing the Prophet as not rich, and Allah's statement that He would have given disbelievers silver roofs.

outline.heading: Zukhruf: shine without substance, and how youth measure success
outline.gist: Zukhruf is what glitters outside but has no value inside; we must not let the young judge success only by followers, fame and money.

outline.heading: Why Quranic stories are never repeated identically
outline.gist: Each retelling, including Musa's story coming next, emphasizes what serves its surah's theme, with subtle differences beyond human composition.

outline.heading: Interlude
Turning away from al-Rahman: seeing only what shines
outline.gist: The verb describes one who can see only in bright light; al-Rahman is used because it is a purely spiritual name of all-encompassing mercy.

outline.heading: Materialism is never satisfied
outline.gist: The materialist moves from one shiny thing to the next and would want the moon after owning the planet; we are all susceptible unless we keep reassessing our worldview.

outline.heading: When people can no longer hear it
outline.gist: Some are simply not there yet and need time; others' past choices have closed them off, and all you can do is make dua for them.

outline.heading: The appointed devil: a catalogue of temptations
outline.gist: A jinn devil only keeps showing options until you take one; that is the extent of his power.

outline.heading: No possession: send people to mental health care
outline.gist: He rejects the idea of jinn taking control of a person; such cases need a mental health specialist, not an exorcist, and he will report those who refuse.

outline.heading: The young man harmed by an exorcism
outline.gist: A young man with family schizophrenia was beaten with a radio during an exorcism and nearly took his own life; once told a devil is inside, a paranoid patient can hardly be convinced otherwise.

outline.heading: Families who refuse treatment
outline.gist: Often the family, not the patient, resists care; the community must escalate such cases to save lives.

outline.heading: The devil learns your key
outline.gist: Devils find what you love and open the matching page; for the materialist it is whatever shines, and the companion never leaves.

outline.heading: Human devils are far worse
outline.gist: The plotting of Shaytan is weak, but human companions are relentless, and no one walks into materialism alone.

outline.heading: Led astray while thinking they are guided
outline.gist: The most frightening part is that they believe they are right and everyone else deluded.

outline.heading: A masjid is not a business
outline.gist: A masjid's success cannot be measured in money; it is a house for those who need service, help and serenity among Muslims.

outline.heading: The Prophet's masjid and Ahl al-Suffah
outline.gist: The poorest lived in the Prophet's masjid day and night and he lived beside them; Abu Hurayrah learned so much because he had nothing else to do.

outline.heading: Measured by people, not buildings; what if it's me?
outline.gist: Even with wealth after Mecca they never built it up, because a masjid is its service and love; he fears the verse may describe himself.

outline.heading: Guarding against it with a holistic view
outline.gist: Check that your perspective is healthy and uses more than one metric, so you are not fooled by what shines.

outline.heading: Interlude
Wishing for the distance of the two easts
outline.gist: On the Day of Judgment, with values set right, he wishes he had been as far from his companion as east from west; Arabs name paired things by one of them in the dual.

outline.heading: Shared punishment brings no relief
outline.gist: Disowning your companion then is too late; each is punished for his own wrong.

outline.heading: You cannot make the deaf hear
outline.gist: The Prophet stayed up looking for ways to reach people, but you cannot force sight or hearing on those who chose against it.

outline.heading: You may die before seeing success
outline.gist: In this Meccan surah the Prophet is told he may die before the message triumphs; demanding guaranteed success would itself be a materialistic outlook.

outline.heading: Success is not judged by outcomes
outline.gist: Measure whether work is done properly, not only whether it succeeds, as a prophet who comes on Judgment Day with no followers was still not a failure.

outline.heading: Hold fast to what was revealed
outline.gist: The Prophet's job is to grip revelation like steel and walk the straight path with integrity, which is not closed-mindedness, whether or not fruits appear.

outline.heading: Interlude
The question you will be asked
outline.gist: You will be asked whether you held on and never sold out your values, not how famous or wealthy you became.

outline.heading: Ask the messengers: nothing else is worth worship
outline.gist: Every earlier messenger would say nothing besides Allah was worth worship or devotion; all else is illusion.

outline.heading: Outro

62:2.ar: هُوَ ٱلَّذِي بَعَثَ فِي ٱلۡأُمِّيِّـۧنَ رَسُولࣰ ا مِّنۡهُمۡ يَتۡلُواْ عَلَيۡهِمۡ ءَايَٰتِهِۦ وَيُزَكِّيهِمۡ وَيُعَلِّمُهُمُ ٱلۡكِتَٰبَ وَٱلۡحِكۡمَةَ وَإِن كَانُواْ مِن قَبۡلُ لَفِي ضَلَٰلࣲ مُّبِينࣲ‏
62:2.en: It is He who has sent among the unlettered a Messenger from themselves reciting to them His verses and purifying them and teaching them the Book and wisdom - although they were before in clear error

62:5.ar: مَثَلُ ٱلَّذِينَ حُمِّلُواْ ٱلتَّوۡرَىٰةَ ثُمَّ لَمۡ يَحۡمِلُوهَا كَمَثَلِ ٱلۡحِمَارِ يَحۡمِلُ أَسۡفَارَۢاۚ بِئۡسَ مَثَلُ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلَّذِينَ كَذَّبُواْ بِـَٔايَٰتِ ٱللَّهِۚ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يَهۡدِي ٱلۡقَوۡمَ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
62:5.en: The example of those who were entrusted with the Torah and then did not take it on is like that of a donkey who carries volumes [of books]. Wretched is the example of the people who deny the signs of Allah. And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people

cYhGAsGy0io.title: Friday Sermon Workshop, Session 1: Why Jumuah and What a Khutbah Is For
cYhGAsGy0io.one_line: Opening session: public speaking as the engine of change, the sanctity and difficulty of the minbar, what audiences want, and changing one behavior.
cYhGAsGy0io.summary: The first session of his Friday Sermon Workshop lays out the theory behind effective speaking. He argues that public speaking has always been the engine of social change and the one trait effective leaders share, good or bad, and that Muslims own the strongest speaking venue in existence yet waste it. He traces Jumuah back to the pre-Islamic gathering day renamed by the Prophet's ancestor, describes the Prophet's reputation for eloquence and his shift from a soft-spoken private manner to a fiery minbar persona, and insists that every khatib stands in for the Messenger and is held to his standard. Jumuah is the hardest form of speaking: no props, no walking, Arabic requirements, a time limit, and an audience of everyone that Allah gathers for you, though that luck can run out as it did for emptied churches. Audiences want four things: to relate, to connect, answers and solutions. The speaker wants one thing: changed behavior, pursued by focusing on a single measurable behavior, painting a vivid picture of both outcomes, and leading by example. He derives the goals of the khutbah from Surat al-Jumu'ah and closes with the attributes of a successful speaker: knowledge, preparation, articulation, focus, confidence without arrogance, honesty, relevance, observation and piety.

outline.heading: Opening
Theory, then trying and failing
outline.gist: He disclaims being a great speaker; what matters is understanding the theory of what makes a good speaker, then trying, failing and trying again until you find your own zone.

outline.heading: Public speaking as the engine of social change
outline.gist: Every major movement in history, civil rights, religious or political, was fuelled by great speakers. Muslims have the most solid speaking venue in the world and still fail to produce the change they hope for.

outline.heading: The one trait effective leaders share
outline.gist: Effective leaders, good or evil, have only public speaking in common: the Prophet and Hitler share nothing else, and even a president with no ethics or plan moved the public from a podium.

outline.heading: From the day of 'Arubah to Jumu'ah
outline.gist: Arabs already gathered on that day in markets to hear poetry and sermons; one of the Prophet's ancestors renamed it Jumu'ah, the gathering, so Islam built on an existing speaking venue.

outline.heading: The Prophet's reputation for eloquence
outline.gist: Even Arabs who died rejecting him knew him for fasahah and khatabah: he could stand anywhere without preparation and speak the high Arabic that only poets and leaders commanded.

outline.heading: Soft-spoken in private, fiery on the minbar
outline.gist: Privately calm, quiet and tender, on the minbar his voice rose and his face reddened as if warning of an army behind the hill, as Jabir describes. Showmanship is fine in its proper context: the minbar calls for a different register.

outline.heading: Standing in for the Messenger
outline.gist: Every minbar is the Messenger's. His own ritual before each khutbah is to remember he is filling in for him and ask what he would think and say about this situation; that sanctity has been forgotten.

outline.heading: Why Jumuah is the hardest form of speaking
outline.gist: Few khutbahs anywhere are memorable because the form is restricted: limited props and slides, no walking around, few gestures, required Arabic verses, a set structure, a time limit and set content.

outline.heading: Speaking to everybody
outline.gist: Public speaking 101 demands a target audience, but the khatib addresses everyone at once; master Jumuah and every other kind of speaking becomes easier.

outline.heading: Jumuah is inseparable from leadership
outline.gist: Wherever two or three Muslims settle, even in a small Alaskan town, they set up a minbar to find each other and keep direction. The Prophet and then the caliphs, some of them weak speakers, gave the khutbah as leaders; sucking leadership out of Jumuah left communities aimless.

outline.heading: Allah gathers them; you only deliver
outline.gist: A dars draws fifty people while Jumuah draws a thousand because Allah obliges them to come; the khatib's job is to offer something worth their time, with understanding, answers and a plan.

outline.heading: The luck can run out
outline.gist: The Prophet warned that what befell the People of the Book will likely befall us: like emptied churches and synagogues, masjids can empty unless people find something meaningful.

outline.heading: They come for Jumuah, not for you
outline.gist: Knowing nobody came to hear him is humbling. Jumuah is obligatory even if the khutbah is in a language you do not understand, and the khutbah is part of the prayer itself, not just a speech.

outline.heading: What the audience wants: four things
outline.gist: Listeners want to relate to the content, connect with the speaker, get answers to their questions and solutions to their problems; leaving with none of the four is a wasted hour.

outline.heading: Relate: live outside the masjid walls
outline.gist: Imams who have lived between the masjid walls for ten years cannot say anything relevant. When he came to Canada he had to discard hundreds of examples and seerah parallels; the first one he tried met total silence.

outline.heading: Connect with the person
outline.gist: Connection is separate from relevance and depends on delivery; you need not reach everyone, only enough people that the rest feel it, and a speaker who connects with no one knows it within minutes.

outline.heading: Answers woven into the talk
outline.gist: Keep an ear to the ground for common questions and insert the answers throughout the talk; stating 'here is the question, here is the answer' kills most of the impact.

outline.heading: Solutions, the hardest of the four
outline.gist: A real solution is almost impossible in a 15 to 20 minute khutbah, but the talk must at least take steps in a direction.

outline.heading: What the speaker wants: changed behavior
outline.gist: Everything else serves one goal, changing people's behavior, including your own. Never speak on trivial topics like water over soda; behavior never changes by accident, only when changing it is the goal, as it was for the Prophet.

outline.heading: Focus on one behavior
outline.gist: Talk about one behavior, not five or six, and keep drilling that one change until you see its effect in people's lives; he admits he still drifts when excited.

outline.heading: Make the change measurable
outline.gist: Give people a valid, tangible way to tell whether the behavior is improving or worsening in their own lives; this is the most often missed point.

outline.heading: Paint a vivid picture of both futures
outline.gist: Describe the problem, what it should look like, and what happens if nothing changes, as the Quran does through its stories. When societies do not change, it is because their speakers have not painted the picture.

outline.heading: Measuring change: ikhlas and anger
outline.gist: Asked what measurable means, he gives ikhlas as a hard case that still has valid measures, and anger as an easy one: how many times a week do I lose my temper.

outline.heading: Lead by example: held to the Prophet's standard
outline.gist: Whoever stands on the Prophet's minbar is judged by his example and can no longer excuse himself like everyone else; if you are not ready, stand behind. The stakes and the reward are both high, and Allah addressed even the Prophet sternly when people's words affected him.

outline.heading: Goal one: recite the signs and explain the creed
outline.gist: Surat al-Jumu'ah sets the khutbah's purposes. First, tell people who Allah is through His signs so they understand their creed and their relationship with Him.

outline.heading: Goal two: purify the hearts
outline.gist: Yuzakkihim: cleanse people's insides and change how they think, which changes how they feel and then how they behave.

outline.heading: Goal three: rulings with wisdom
outline.gist: Teach what is halal and what is not, with the hikmah to know which ruling applies now and which later.

outline.heading: Goal four: raise real awareness
outline.gist: The surah then describes those who carry information without understanding; the khutbah must truly educate and enlighten.

outline.heading: Goal five: action over lineage
outline.gist: Against the claim of being the children of Musa and Ibrahim, stress that only action counts, not background, family or wealth.

outline.heading: Goal six: remind of accountability
outline.gist: The surah ends on accountability. Allah did not leave the khutbah as a vague 'reminder'; its elements are spelled out in the surah named after it.

outline.heading: Course theory, part one: delivery
outline.gist: About six theory sessions before practice, starting with delivery: body language, tone, voice, sitting or standing, moving, gestures and props, which matter more than what is said.

outline.heading: Course theory, part two: content needs a twist
outline.gist: What content suits a Jumuah and other settings; everyone has heard every topic many times, so if you have no twist, pick something else.

outline.heading: Course theory, part three: Jumuah specifics
outline.gist: Jumuah has many specifics, such as dress code: give it in jeans and people will talk about nothing else, so close the holes people can poke at.

outline.heading: Improvising: his teacher's surprise topic
outline.gist: Practice will include prepared talks and improvisation. His teacher, as they pulled up for a condolence visit, told him to speak on the long hadith in Musnad Ahmad about death; he bombed, but learned to structure thoughts fast and later produced poetry on the spot when he had nothing prepared.

outline.heading: Feedback and styles
outline.gist: Learning to take feedback matters; he will speak first and invite them to tear his talk apart, then try different styles and scenarios.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute one: knowledge
outline.gist: Never explain what you do not understand yourself, say 'I don't know' when needed, and build knowledge for life; many khatibs lack knowledge of the world more than of the Sharia. He points to a long Arabic public-speaking series and Stephen Covey.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute two: preparation
outline.gist: Out of respect for any audience he always prepares, even ten minutes for a topic he has given for years or a family gathering.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute three: articulation
outline.gist: Command of English or Arabic, vocabulary and grammar is the first thing people hear; strong articulation can carry a speaker who lacks the other tools.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute four: focus
outline.gist: Stay on one topic from several angles and avoid istitrad, digression, which he confesses is his own habit.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute five: confidence, not arrogance
outline.gist: The line is thin; if you cannot hit confidence, come off shaky rather than arrogant, because people sympathize with the first and reject the second.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute six: honesty and credibility
outline.gist: People sniff out a hypocrite almost immediately; if you do not believe and live what you say, they feel it.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute seven: relevance
outline.gist: Speak to people according to what they know, their age, background and experience.

outline.heading: The village imam who preached love to farmers
outline.gist: A soft-hearted young imam in his Syrian mountain village reached no one with talks on love until, on his advice, he warned of seventy years' fall in Jahannam for denying daughters their inheritance; six rows came to Fajr, and he stayed ten years. Know your audience's nature.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute eight: observation
outline.gist: Read every person every moment and adjust: move on when they are bored, clarify when they are lost. Masks make this hard, forcing him to read eyes alone.

outline.heading: Speaker attribute nine: piety and leading by example
outline.gist: Practise what you preach; you need not be perfect, but never tell people to do what you are not doing yourself.

outline.heading: Outro

GBgQ1Xgzk78.title: Friday Sermon Workshop, Session 2: Vocal Delivery
GBgQ1Xgzk78.one_line: Workshop session on using the voice: speed and repetition, vocalizing emotion, clarity, tone, humor and seriousness, slang, and the power of the pause.
GBgQ1Xgzk78.summary: Second session of his Friday Sermon Workshop, the first on delivery. He opens with Mehrabian's 7/38/55 rule: content captures only seven percent of an audience's attention, so deep scholars go unheard while empty performers draw millions of views, and the point of learning showmanship is to let the seven percent of content arrive. He names four bad habits (always high, always low, too loud, too sharp) and then four rules. Speed: slow beats fast, but vary pace to signal what matters, as the Quran does when it tells the same story at different lengths, and repeat key sentences functionally as the Prophet repeated things three times. Emotion: the voice must carry sadness, anger, happiness, mockery, questions and surprise, and sarcasm that is not vocalized clearly backfires. Clarity: enunciate every letter and check pronunciation, especially for an audience whose first language is not English or Arabic. Tone: never stay monotonic more than ten to fifteen seconds, but never exaggerate, because listeners detect anything not genuine. He adds tips: imitate a speaker you admire until you break off into your own style, cut filler ticks, use humor only when it serves the point and never at the start or end, learn to shift into seriousness, use a little slang, and master silence, since public speaking is the art of the pause.

outline.heading: Opening
The 7/38/55 rule
outline.gist: In Mehrabian's rule, content earns only 7 percent of an audience's attention, voice 38 and body language 55. Scholars with mind-blowing content go unheard while performers with nothing to say get millions of views.

outline.heading: Bad vocalization one: always high
outline.gist: A voice pitched high the whole time makes people scroll past within seconds, even when the message matters.

outline.heading: Bad vocalization two: always low
outline.gist: Staying deep and low the whole time loses people too; the skill is moving up and down to suit what you emphasize.

outline.heading: Bad vocalization three: too loud
outline.gist: He admits this is his own fault: getting passionate and yelling for seven or eight minutes. Loudness works only for a few moments.

outline.heading: Bad vocalization four: too sharp
outline.gist: A sharp sound, often from microphone distance or volume settings, makes everyone cringe.

outline.heading: His machine-gun speed
outline.gist: Years ago he spoke so fast that older men stopped him mid-talk to make him repeat everything. You learn the rules and improve; what remains becomes your persona.

outline.heading: Rule one, speed: slow beats fast
outline.gist: When in doubt go slower; it costs you 15 to 30 percent of your content and slowing your words slows your thinking, but people understand and enjoy you more.

outline.heading: Speed for emphasis: the Quran's retellings
outline.gist: Jog through the context and slow down at the point. The Quran keeps every element of a story but gives Musa's encounter with Pharaoh fifty verses in one surah and two in another, depending on the point there.

outline.heading: Slow down on the Prophet's words
outline.gist: Narrate the setting of a hadith quickly, then say his words slowly and clearly; otherwise people leave knowing they heard a story but not why.

outline.heading: Repetition: the Prophet's threefold pattern
outline.gist: The Prophet repeated things three times, but never identically; each repetition pushed people to think further. He demonstrates a functional threefold repetition.

outline.heading: Repeat one key sentence
outline.gist: Good speakers choose a sentence that matters and repeat it in different ways through the talk so the audience leaves with it memorized; fast speakers especially need repetition.

outline.heading: Rule two, emotion: sadness
outline.gist: The voice must carry the emotion. For sadness, such as the Prophet weeping over his son Ibrahim, come down, slow and leave space; khatibs who yell while crying are playing on emotion.

outline.heading: Emotion: anger
outline.gist: Anger goes louder, sharper and abrupt, as in the Prophet's rebuke when companions traded racist insults: leave it, it is rotten.

outline.heading: Why khatibs sound angry
outline.gist: The Prophet's minbar persona was loud and seemed angry because he addressed critical matters and wanted people alert and ready for change, not laid back.

outline.heading: Emotion: happiness
outline.gist: Happiness lifts the voice higher.

outline.heading: His mother followed a speaker by his voice alone
outline.gist: His mother could not follow a speaker's dialect yet understood everything from the rise and fall of his voice: good vocalization carries meaning even when the words do not.

outline.heading: Emotion: mockery and sarcasm
outline.gist: Mockery needs its own voice, as when the chiefs taunted Nuh building the ark: you were a prophet, now a carpenter.

outline.heading: When sarcasm backfired
outline.gist: A listener took his sarcastic khutbah line about the cartoons of the Prophet literally and confronted him. Sarcasm says the opposite of the message, so it must sound clearly different from your normal voice, or leave it.

outline.heading: Emotion: questions
outline.gist: Questions rise at the end; scholars even taught that questions in the Quran should be recited as questions, though that is hard to do in prayer.

outline.heading: Emotion: surprise
outline.gist: After building suspense, surprise needs an abrupt change in tone, volume or nature of the voice; done well it can make the whole speech.

outline.heading: Rule three, clarity: enunciation
outline.gist: Clarity matters most for audiences hearing a second language. Every letter must come out, unlike the joke about the man who drops last letters; tajweed is training in exactly this.

outline.heading: Clarity: pronunciation
outline.gist: Say words the way your audience is used to hearing them; Muhammad Hamou listed every word he mispronounced when he arrived. Clear enunciation and pronunciation alone can carry a speaker for years.

outline.heading: Rule four, tone: never monotonic
outline.gist: Monotony is a main reason people sleep in Jumuah. Never hold one tone more than 10 to 15 seconds; ideally the tone moves within every sentence.

outline.heading: Don't exaggerate: stay genuine
outline.gist: Exaggerated tone changes bother him most: people detect anything not genuine and stop listening. Showmanship exists only so the seven percent of content arrives; this is not theater or stand-up comedy.

outline.heading: Imitate a speaker, then break off
outline.gist: Watch speakers you admire for how they deliver, not what they say, and imitate them until you develop your own recipe; every reciter with a good Quran voice imitated someone, and those who did not read dully all their lives.

outline.heading: Drop your filler ticks
outline.gist: Fillers like 'you know' or 'fa-mma' repeated endlessly signal uncertainty. His own is 'yani', even in medical interviews; a sheikh who always said 'na'am' said it in prayer when corrected and confused everyone.

outline.heading: Humor: never open or close with a joke
outline.gist: Humor is the most dangerous tool: a joke that bombs at the start ends the talk, never sell a joke before telling it, and a failed closing joke is the cow kicking over the milk pail.

outline.heading: Humor must be functional
outline.gist: A joke inside the talk must serve the sequence of thought, never be thrown in just to make people laugh.

outline.heading: Topics never to joke about
outline.gist: Disabilities, religions, catastrophes, looks, weight and anything that can sound sexist, especially from a Muslim man; second-wife jokes, most of his own repertoire, are off the table.

outline.heading: Laughter and tears, as with the Prophet
outline.gist: He rarely jokes, but the companions said the Prophet made them laugh and cry; drawing both emotions naturally relaxes people and makes them listen.

outline.heading: Shifting into seriousness
outline.gist: Seriousness does not need a stern face or a sharp voice; it is the shift from a laid-back story to raising the tension in the room, moving back and forth between humor and gravity using speed, emotion and tone.

outline.heading: Attention spans have collapsed
outline.gist: Songs are three minutes and talks online must be under ten to be heard, so speakers need every tool. In his father's youth a village hakawati held everyone with made-up stories because there was nothing else.

outline.heading: In Arabic: fusha with a safe sukun
outline.gist: Speak fusha, and if unsure of a case ending put a sukun on the last letter; back home a wrong vowel on the minbar could end you, and he once saw a khatib corrected mid-khutbah.

outline.heading: A little slang, as the Prophet used Habashi words
outline.gist: In English, a few words a particular group uses win their attention, never profanity. The Prophet learned Habashi words such as 'sanah' and used them with Abyssinian Muslims so they felt included.

outline.heading: The art of the pause
outline.gist: Public speaking is the art of the pause: a few seconds of silence lets people weigh what you said, anticipate what comes, and absorb it. Do not fill every second.

outline.heading: Why the Prophet sat between the two khutbahs
outline.gist: He reads the sitting as a moment for listeners to hear their own thoughts, since they cannot listen to you and to themselves at once.

outline.heading: Pause without looking lost
outline.gist: Too much silence is awkward; even when your mind goes blank, pause so it does not look like forgetting. Stop just before your most important word, and never fill gaps with 'um'.

outline.heading: Get comfortable with silence
outline.gist: Like a therapist at ease in a quiet room, a speaker must be comfortable with silence; we are rarely silent in life. Try telling a story with and without pauses.

outline.heading: Recap: four questions while speaking
outline.gist: Avoid the four bad vocalizations except for deliberate moments, and always know your speed, emotion, clarity and tone. Look up any word you cannot pronounce, as he did for 'hoopoe'; stay diverse with humor, seriousness and slang; use the pause, which he admits he uses too little.

outline.heading: Outro

38:22.en: When they entered upon David and he was alarmed by them? They said, "Fear not. [We are] two adversaries, one of whom has wronged the other, so judge between us with truth and do not exceed [it] and guide us to the sound path

ihEhEMP5FZQ.title: Seerah Ep 24: Ja'far Before the Najashi
ihEhEMP5FZQ.one_line: The migration to Abyssinia, Quraysh's embassy to the Najashi, and Ja'far's five-point defence of the Muslims as a model of persuasive speech.
ihEhEMP5FZQ.summary: He frames the migration to Abyssinia as a deliberate strategic move: the Prophet opened a second base on another continent, put Quraysh under moral pressure from other Arab tribes and from families who had lost their children, and kept the initiative rather than reacting, which he contrasts with an ummah that has stopped planning. He stresses that the Prophet sent nobles and his own daughter alongside the weak, showing there is no class divide among believers, and that true leadership never leaves the struggling behind. When Amr ibn al-As paints the emigrants as reckless youth, the Najashi insists on hearing the other side; he links this to the story of Dawud and the two litigants and warns young people about algorithmic bubbles and forwarded misinformation. The heart of the session is Ja'far's speech: a short, planned, five-part case built on values the king already shared, ending with a sincere compliment to his justice, followed by the recitation of Surah Maryam that moved the court to tears. He asks listeners to speak with structure, relevance to the audience and brevity, to verify what they hear, and to care for the weakest in the community.

outline.heading: Nobles and his own daughter sent with the weak
outline.gist: No socio-economic segregation among believers; none of the wealthy objected to going.

outline.heading: Leadership that never leaves the weak behind
outline.gist: The Prophet lived like the poorest when he could not lift them; communities lose unity when the struggling are left behind.

outline.heading: Amr's case: reckless youth who left every religion
outline.gist: A skilled diplomat primes the king to see the Muslims as troublemakers whose elders want them back.

outline.heading: Hear both sides: the judge and the injured eye
outline.gist: A judge refuses to rule on one dramatic complaint because the other party may be worse off.

outline.heading: Dawud and the two litigants
outline.gist: Startled in his prayer, Dawud ruled after hearing only one side; the test was about listening to the other party.

outline.heading: Algorithmic bubbles and forwarded falsehoods
outline.gist: Social media feeds our biases and makes hatred easy; the young generation has no excuse not to sift and verify.

outline.heading: The Najashi summons the Muslims
outline.gist: The king asks what faith brought them, neither his nor their fathers'.

outline.heading: Ja'far's elevator pitch and speaking to context
outline.gist: Explaining Islam depends on time, place and audience; a rambling, irrelevant presentation loses the listener.

outline.heading: Ja'far under pressure
outline.gist: A young man who most resembled the Prophet has seconds to frame a narrative that will save a hundred lives.

outline.heading: Public speaking: know your points by heart
outline.gist: Plan the sequence of points before speaking and master the material rather than reading cards.

outline.heading: Point one: what we were in jahiliyyah
outline.gist: Ja'far listed wrongs the king already recognised as wrong, appealing to universal values rather than unfamiliar rituals.

outline.heading: Point two: who the Prophet is
outline.gist: One of us, of known lineage, honesty and trustworthiness.

outline.heading: Point three: what he taught us
outline.gist: Worship of Allah alone with honesty, kinship, care for neighbours and the weak, all things the king would endorse.

outline.heading: Point four: our people persecuted us
outline.gist: Turning attention to what the two envoys' own people had done.

outline.heading: Point five: we came hoping in your justice
outline.gist: An honest compliment to the king closes the case; the court waits in tension.

outline.heading: Surah Maryam recited in the court
outline.gist: Asked for revelation, Ja'far recites Maryam; the king and his court weep and refuse to hand the Muslims over.

outline.heading: Stop before people get bored
outline.gist: Ja'far stopped at the right point in the surah; Amr plans a second round.

43:20.ar: وَقَالُواْ لَوۡ شَآءَ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنُ مَا عَبَدۡنَٰهُمۗ مَّا لَهُم بِذَٰلِكَ مِنۡ عِلۡمٍۖ إِنۡ هُمۡ إِلَّا يَخۡرُصُونَ
43:20.en: And they said, "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them." They have of that no knowledge. They are not but falsifying

43:21.ar: أَمۡ ءَاتَيۡنَٰهُمۡ كِتَٰبࣰ ا مِّن قَبۡلِهِۦ فَهُم بِهِۦ مُسۡتَمۡسِكُونَ
43:21.en: Or have We given them a book before the Qur'an to which they are adhering

43:22.ar: بَلۡ قَالُوٓاْ إِنَّا وَجَدۡنَآ ءَابَآءَنَا عَلَىٰٓ أُمَّةࣲ وَإِنَّا عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَٰرِهِم مُّهۡتَدُونَ
43:22.en: Rather, they say, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and we are in their footsteps [rightly] guided

43:23.ar: وَكَذَٰلِكَ مَآ أَرۡسَلۡنَا مِن قَبۡلِكَ فِي قَرۡيَةࣲ مِّن نَّذِيرٍ إِلَّا قَالَ مُتۡرَفُوهَآ إِنَّا وَجَدۡنَآ ءَابَآءَنَا عَلَىٰٓ أُمَّةࣲ وَإِنَّا عَلَىٰٓ ءَاثَٰرِهِم مُّقۡتَدُونَ
43:23.en: And similarly, We did not send before you any warner into a city except that its affluent said, "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and we are, in their footsteps, following

43:24.ar: ۞قَٰلَ أَوَلَوۡ جِئۡتُكُم بِأَهۡدَىٰ مِمَّا وَجَدتُّمۡ عَلَيۡهِ ءَابَآءَكُمۡۖ قَالُوٓاْ إِنَّا بِمَآ أُرۡسِلۡتُم بِهِۦ كَٰفِرُونَ
43:24.en: [Each warner] said, "Even if I brought you better guidance than that [religion] upon which you found your fathers?" They said, "Indeed we, in that with which you were sent, are disbelievers

43:26.ar: وَإِذۡ قَالَ إِبۡرَٰهِيمُ لِأَبِيهِ وَقَوۡمِهِۦٓ إِنَّنِي بَرَآءࣱ مِّمَّا تَعۡبُدُونَ

TAQQk3gny_8.title: Az-Zukhruf, Verses 20-30 (Fajr Dars)
TAQQk3gny_8.one_line: The fatalist excuse and free will, speaking for Allah without knowledge, blind loyalty to ancestral custom, and Ibrahim leaving a lasting word behind.
TAQQk3gny_8.summary: He recaps the surah's warning against one-dimensional materialistic thinking, recalling how early Muslims stood out for honouring women while today consumer culture teaches young people that only wealth and fame mean success. Verse 20's claim that the idolaters worship by Allah's will is the old fatalist argument: it assumes Allah knows the future the way we do, by programming, as with a wind-up car or the failed pandemic projections. Allah knows every possible choice while we remain free. Verse 21's demand for a book leads him to the gravity of speaking on Allah's behalf, his own greatest fear as a teacher, and to the hadith of the man who swore Allah would not forgive another: no one may use the Quran as a catalogue of who goes to Hell. Verses 22-25 show the affluent always defending ancestral custom because it serves them, which he sees today in costly cultural marriage customs that leave young people unmarried into their thirties. Islam was never rejected on theology alone; there is always a personal hook. The mukadhdhib saw the truth and refused it, unlike someone shown a distorted Islam. Ibrahim rejected the rigged religion of Ur and left a word behind as a seed, the model for persistent, patient dawah, even with teenagers who seem not to listen.

outline.heading: Recap: the Ha-Mim cluster and its three warnings
outline.gist: Surahs sharing the same opening letters share a theme; Az-Zukhruf warns against what glitters without substance and the one-dimensional materialistic view behind much bad judgment.

outline.heading: Recap: women valued only for financial benefit
outline.gist: In Jahiliyyah women were devalued because they did not add warriors or wealth to the tribe, a mentality the Quran changed.

outline.heading: When Muslims led on women's rights
outline.gist: A Muslim of the Prophet's era stood out for how he treated women: rights to believe, learn, voice an opinion, inherit, own and trade, and equal accountability before Allah, long before other societies. Muslims have since regressed.

outline.heading: Consumer culture is framing young minds
outline.gist: The same narrow outlook rules today, which is why he chose this surah; consumerism is shaping what young people hope for, fear and call success.

outline.heading: Your father still made it
outline.gist: A father without a million followers who worked hard and held a family together is a success; making wealth and fame the only markers is a calamity, and the Quran addresses this head on.

outline.heading: If the Most Merciful had willed: the fatalist excuse
outline.gist: After reciting, he explains their claim that they worship idols by Allah's will, the age-old argument of compulsion, which ignores that Allah can create a creature with free will.

outline.heading: Free will is no threat to Allah
outline.gist: Nothing the creature does escapes Him; the materialist can only judge by his own simple experience, so the verse says they are merely guessing.

outline.heading: Kharas: the farmer's estimate
outline.gist: Kharas is how farmers back home estimated the fruit on a tree to pay the landowner up front, a guess rather than a count; their claim is just as unfounded.

outline.heading: We can only predict what has no choice
outline.gist: We foresee only what follows an algorithm, like a wind-up car aimed at a pillar; forecasts of human behaviour remain estimates that people keep breaking.

outline.heading: The pandemic and the limits of prediction
outline.gist: Two years of failed graphs and projections eroded trust in the medical system and governments, showing how little we can predict.

outline.heading: He knows, yet you are free
outline.gist: If Allah's knowledge worked like ours the fatalists would be right; it does not, and that difference is exactly what makes Him God.

outline.heading: Every possible option is known to Him
outline.gist: Borrowing the idea of infinite parallel universes: Allah knows every option open to you at each moment, and you simply choose among them, so you can never surprise Him.

outline.heading: Did We give them a book before this?
outline.gist: Their claim rests on no knowledge and no scripture; Allah asks where it came from.

outline.heading: The danger of speaking for Allah
outline.gist: Attributing to Allah what is untrue or unknown is among the gravest sins; anyone explaining the Quran must think a hundred times, because a mistake spreads and letting ego or agenda in is the worst corruption.

outline.heading: Who gave you permission?
outline.gist: Allah challenges them to show the book that says He compels people, and asks who authorised them to speak on His behalf.

outline.heading: The man who swore Allah would not forgive
outline.gist: Allah forgave the sinner and held the one who spoke for Him to account; reciting a warning is very different from applying it to people.

outline.heading: The Quran is not a catalogue of the damned
outline.gist: Syllogisms like 'every mushrik enters the Fire, so this person will' do not apply; declaring someone's destination puts you at terrible risk.

outline.heading: Where people end up is Allah's business
outline.gist: We may only name a destination Allah or the Prophet named, as with Abu Lahab; the next verse turns to their real motive.

outline.heading: We found our fathers on a way
outline.gist: Their real problem was the ease of the status quo, especially when it is inherited and financially beneficial; then it becomes almost impossible to change.

outline.heading: Custom outlives even harm
outline.gist: Even harmful cultural traditions resist change; ummah here means a collective way of life the forefathers lived.

outline.heading: The affluent always resist the warner
outline.gist: Every warner was opposed first by the comfortable, who did not care who was oppressed so long as it was not them; the pattern persists today in new forms.

outline.heading: Marriage held hostage by culture
outline.gist: Cultural costs and celebrations leave men and women unmarried into their thirties, though the Prophet married people with Quran as the dowry.

outline.heading: The question no one asks
outline.gist: Delaying marriage fifteen years past puberty while turning a blind eye, for the sake of family prestige, is worse than Jahiliyyah because we know the alternative.

outline.heading: Complaining about mahr, then demanding it
outline.gist: A father protests the dowry demanded for his son, then years later imposes the same on his daughter's suitor: the same materialistic logic.

outline.heading: Even if I brought better guidance?
outline.gist: Every warner offered something better than ancestral habit, and they replied they reject whatever he was sent with without hearing it.

outline.heading: Islam was never rejected on theology
outline.gist: Like Salih's people, they refused because change threatened prestige and income; he finds no case in the Quran or Sunnah of rejection on theology alone.

outline.heading: Find the hook
outline.gist: In his conversations with doubters he looks for the personal experience or misunderstanding behind the objection, because the theology of one Creator beyond time and space is simple and beautiful.

outline.heading: The mukadhdhib saw the truth and refused it
outline.gist: Unlike the general term kafir, the mukadhdhib recognised the right way and refused it for self-interest, which earns the severest punishment.

outline.heading: Those shown a distorted Islam
outline.gist: People who rejected a badly presented Islam will likely find mercy; we deal with others at face value but cannot know their backstory or judge their end.

outline.heading: Ibrahim's Ur, the great city of its age
outline.gist: He recites Ibrahim's verses and describes Ur in southern Iraq near today's Nasiriyah, a crowded centre of knowledge and power with temple-towers built on high ground.

outline.heading: A rigged religion of kings and clergy
outline.gist: Gods of moon, sun and rain, some reachable only through costly offerings to priests, kept everyone controlled; Ibrahim saw it as a game run by liars.

outline.heading: Free of what you worship, except my Creator
outline.gist: Ibrahim disowned their gods except the One who created him and will guide him; they expelled him, yet he left those words behind him.

outline.heading: Breaking the idols
outline.gist: Their offerings fed corrupt clergy and kings; he broke the idols, left the axe on the biggest, and exposed that they worship what cannot speak.

outline.heading: Leave a seed behind
outline.gist: They knew they were wrong but too much was at stake, so they threw him in the fire; still he left a lasting word, and that is the Muslim's duty in dawah.

outline.heading: Teenagers who come back years later
outline.gist: Youth work can be draining when they mock and ignore you, but people he had given up on returned years later recalling his words; say the genuine, kind word anyway.

outline.heading: Comfort as the real obstacle
outline.gist: Ibrahim is the model, and the surah's point is that the people were embedded in inherited wealth and comfort when the clear messenger came.

outline.heading: They called the truth magic
outline.gist: Their rejection followed their financial interest, another example of materialistic judgment.

cfZ4NITZTng.title: Friday Sermon Workshop, Session 3: Body Language
cfZ4NITZTng.one_line: Workshop session on body language: hands, facial expressions, eye contact, posture and movement, plus practical remedies for stage fright.
cfZ4NITZTng.summary: Third session of his Friday Sermon Workshop, recorded during the December 2020 lockdown. He restates the 7/38/55 rule: content captures only seven percent of attention, voice about a third and body language the majority, which is why deep scholars go unheard while clowns draw crowds. He then works through four parts of body language. Hands must move, but every gesture should match the meaning and emotion of the words; sudden movements, repeated tics, synchronized robotic motion and finger pointing all break the connection. The face must be lit and unobstructed, and a speaker should smile at least once so people know he is human. Eye contact should last three to four seconds per person and be spontaneous, because looking is how a speaker reads and adjusts to his audience. For posture: stand, face people, never turn your back or side, move in small steps rather than pacing, and do not clutch your own hand. He notes that Jumuah strips away most of these tools, which is why it is the hardest form of speaking. He closes with remedies for stage fright: hold on to something, look just above the last head, use a personal pre-talk routine of dhikr, deep breath and smile, do not cram beforehand, and practise aloud, even to walls or to your own family at home.

outline.heading: Opening
Body language carries most of the attention
outline.gist: After last session's voice rules he restates that content earns only seven percent of attention, so deep scholars no one can sit through for five minutes go unheard. Body language, in four parts (hands, face, eyes, posture), carries over sixty percent and must be practised clumsily before it works.

outline.heading: Use your hands, though the Arab khatib held a staff
outline.gist: You cannot speak with arms stuck at your sides. Arabs disliked a khatib who gestured, so he held a pole, stick or sword, not to signal war; done that way, Jumuah takes away 70 to 80 percent of body language, so the other tools must be strong.

outline.heading: Gestures must fit the meaning
outline.gist: Saying a man was fat and tall with mismatched hands confuses people. Hands are the most effective part of body language: mute a good speaker and you can still follow the gist.

outline.heading: Why Jumuah strips gestures away
outline.gist: His own theory: Allah removed these enjoyable but distracting tools from Jumuah so the congregation focuses on the content, which otherwise matters little to listeners.

outline.heading: Describing with the hands
outline.gist: When you describe something or say 'we should open our hearts', a matching hand movement makes the listener relate and connect far more.

outline.heading: Gestures carry emotion
outline.gist: Never state your emotion outright; let it come through. Hands coming together bring intensity, closeness or sadness; opening them signals optimism and happiness; touching the face can show fear.

outline.heading: Make every gesture deliberate
outline.gist: No scratching or idle movement; a thought-out gesture, like a hand to the head when someone sees something startling, makes the feeling land. Practice sessions will check that each gesture fits.

outline.heading: Avoid sudden movements
outline.gist: Nearly every gesture has a context where it works, but a sudden one never does: it spikes adrenaline for no reason and makes people uncomfortable. Replace it with a sudden change in voice or face.

outline.heading: The sheikh who banged the minbar
outline.gist: A sheikh from his youth gave hour-long khutbahs, sent people wanting a short one elsewhere, and banged the minbar to wake dozing old men; the bang threw everyone into fight-or-flight. Never force an emotion on the audience.

outline.heading: Avoid repeated mannerisms and robotic symmetry
outline.gist: No windshield-wiper hand repeated for fifteen minutes, no vocal fillers (use silence instead), and no both hands moving in sync; each hand should move on its own, naturally.

outline.heading: Teachers who drilled fixed gestures
outline.gist: Early public-speaking teachers he heard made students memorize set hand movements, and those students spoke all their lives with gestures that carried no meaning or emotion.

outline.heading: Point with the whole hand, not a finger
outline.gist: The Prophet pointed with his full hand; a finger singles people out and invades their space. The same applies to content: say 'we' and 'I' rather than accusing 'you'.

outline.heading: Keep your face well lit
outline.gist: Facial expression is the most underused part of body language; stand where light falls on your face so people can see your expressions.

outline.heading: Trust your instinct when reading faces
outline.gist: Infants read their mothers' faces instantly and we are all wired for it, but we learn to distrust that instinct. If someone close looks distressed, or your teenager looks like he is lying, he is; deal with it before problems pile up.

outline.heading: Nothing between your face and the audience
outline.gist: No masks, no bank of microphones. The minbar was built because crowds grew so large that those at the back could no longer see the Prophet's face; even the livestream camera bothers him for blocking his view of the brothers.

outline.heading: Smile at least once
outline.gist: However heavy the topic, smile at some point, even with a pause, so people know you are human. The Prophet smiled even in Jumuah despite his serious minbar persona.

outline.heading: Keep the smile appropriate
outline.gist: His unusual sense of humor once had an elderly man demand what was funny; smile only where it fits, and in a joke know which part to smile at or the audience laughs at the wrong time.

outline.heading: Don't block your natural expressions
outline.gist: Disgust, happiness, pain and sadness should show on your face. In a coffee shop your face tells the story naturally; at the front, self-consciousness builds walls, and while some emotions need control, not all should be blocked.

outline.heading: His teacher's single tear
outline.gist: People on the autism spectrum struggle to show emotion. A teacher of his, followed by thousands, told moving stories with no expression at all; in ten years the only sign was one tear while recounting the Prophet's death. Those who struggle must consciously practise.

outline.heading: Eyes: a few seconds per person
outline.gist: Hold each person's gaze three to four seconds; longer makes people uncomfortable and singles them out, like a teacher of his who spoke only to him all class; fixing on the same few people loses the room.

outline.heading: Eye contact is how you read the room
outline.gist: Glancing too quickly means you take in nothing; looking is how you see whether people are engaged and adjust tone, pace, posture or material. Masks force him to read eyes alone.

outline.heading: Spontaneous, not systematic
outline.gist: Sweeping the room in a fixed pattern looks robotic, and people do not connect with robots; move from person to person naturally.

outline.heading: Posture: standing beats sitting
outline.gist: Standing raises attention by about 14 percent. He sits for his own halaqahs out of tiredness, and the Prophet gave most talks sitting, so sitting is acceptable, but Jumuah is given standing and standing is always better.

outline.heading: Never turn your back or side
outline.gist: Turning away cuts the connection like pulling the wifi; only do it when acting out a story. The Prophet never turned just his neck to look at something but turned his whole torso.

outline.heading: Stand straight: his first khutbah at a Syrian army camp
outline.gist: At a compulsory summer camp where prayer was banned, a friend pushed him up unprepared to give Jumuah; his left leg drummed audibly, so he leaned on a concrete beam at 45 degrees. Stand straight with no crossed legs or stretching, but if you are shaking, hold something.

outline.heading: Move in a step and half step, never pace
outline.gist: Moving beats standing still, but walking back and forth is useless and unsettling, like a sudden movement. Take a step, then a half step, within a small radius; Jumuah removes this tool too.

outline.heading: Don't hold your hand like it's broken
outline.gist: Clasping one arm as if it needs a cast looks bad; if you are not gesturing, let your hands rest naturally, since a held hand is a tool not being used.

outline.heading: Glossophobia: nerves are normal
outline.gist: Fear of public speaking is the most common phobia; some studies say three quarters of people would rather die than speak. He finds it lower in Canada, where schools train students, than in Syria. A teenager with no nerves at all is the worrying case.

outline.heading: Shaking and sweating are fine
outline.gist: If you shake, hold a chair or anything until you calm down after a few minutes. Sweat as much as you like, but dress so it does not show; baggy clothes help.

outline.heading: Look just above the last head
outline.gist: His trick for four years: look half a metre above the last person and move every two or three seconds. A congregant once felt there was 'some dude behind me'. It costs you the connection and the reading of the room, so use it only until you settle.

outline.heading: Faces are your feedback: this is a service
outline.gist: When someone keeps looking away, something did not work for them; you can figure it out yourself and fix it next time. Speaking is a service, and if it is not helping you sit down or change it.

outline.heading: His routine: dhikr, a deep breath, a smile
outline.gist: Before speaking, say your own adhkar, close your eyes, take a deep breath, smile, then stand up and be yourself; public speaking will change your character over time.

outline.heading: Compensate for what you cannot fix
outline.gist: He once had several people slow him down live until they were satisfied, and at that speed he could no longer think or produce. Know your weakness and make up for it with other strengths, as speakers who cannot stand do.

outline.heading: Imagine something funny
outline.gist: For the very nervous, especially the young: picture the audience with potato heads; laughing inside relaxes you.

outline.heading: Don't review right before
outline.gist: Give whatever you have; for his first six years he delivered under a quarter of what he prepared, and forgetting points will always happen.

outline.heading: Use the bathroom first
outline.gist: Always go before standing in front of people, or your body language will not be the kind you want.

outline.heading: Interlude
A camera is no audience
outline.gist: Speaking to a camera sucks the life out of public speaking: no engagement, no connection, no faces to feel emotion with.

outline.heading: Interlude
Give your khutbah to trees and walls
outline.gist: His teacher told him to speak to trees and walls when there was no one; three times he gave a full halaqah in an empty masjid because he had prepared it, and the caretaker who found him stayed to listen.

outline.heading: Hear yourself and find your balance
outline.gist: Only by speaking aloud do you hear what you dislike and change it. Standing up changes your body's chemistry, so the aim is to bring your natural one-on-one self to the front; some must peel off filters and others tone down overexpression.

outline.heading: Give Jumuah to your family at home
outline.gist: Use the lockdown to hold Jumuah at home and let your son, daughter or wife give it, since the rulings are more flexible at home; if your own children will listen to you, you do not need him.

outline.heading: The rules apply to all speaking but performance
outline.gist: Asked where these rules apply: everywhere except theater, stand-up and musical performance, which have their own laws, always adjusted to context.

themes.note: Performance anxiety: fear of public speaking is the most common phobia, nervousness is healthy and normal, and he gives concrete coping techniques rather than telling people to suppress it.

6:34.ar: وَلَقَدۡ كُذِّبَتۡ رُسُلࣱ مِّن قَبۡلِكَ فَصَبَرُواْ عَلَىٰ مَا كُذِّبُواْ وَأُوذُواْ حَتَّىٰٓ أَتَىٰهُمۡ نَصۡرُنَاۚ وَلَا مُبَدِّلَ لِكَلِمَٰتِ ٱللَّهِۚ وَلَقَدۡ جَآءَكَ مِن نَّبَإِيْ ٱلۡمُرۡسَلِينَ
6:34.en: And certainly were messengers denied before you, but they were patient over [the effects of] denial, and they were harmed until Our victory came to them. And none can alter the words of Allah. And there has certainly come to you some information about the [previous] messengers

6:35.ar: وَإِن كَانَ كَبُرَ عَلَيۡكَ إِعۡرَاضُهُمۡ فَإِنِ ٱسۡتَطَعۡتَ أَن تَبۡتَغِيَ نَفَقࣰ ا فِي ٱلۡأَرۡضِ أَوۡ سُلَّمࣰ ا فِي ٱلسَّمَآءِ فَتَأۡتِيَهُم بِـَٔايَةࣲۚ وَلَوۡ شَآءَ ٱللَّهُ لَجَمَعَهُمۡ عَلَى ٱلۡهُدَىٰۚ فَلَا تَكُونَنَّ مِنَ ٱلۡجَٰهِلِينَ
6:35.en: And if their evasion is difficult for you, then if you are able to seek a tunnel into the earth or a stairway into the sky to bring them a sign, [then do so]. But if Allah had willed, He would have united them upon guidance. So never be of the ignorant

12:110.ar: حَتَّىٰٓ إِذَا ٱسۡتَيۡـَٔسَ ٱلرُّسُلُ وَظَنُّوٓاْ أَنَّهُمۡ قَدۡ كُذِبُواْ جَآءَهُمۡ نَصۡرُنَا فَنُجِّيَ مَن نَّشَآءُۖ وَلَا يُرَدُّ بَأۡسُنَا عَنِ ٱلۡقَوۡمِ ٱلۡمُجۡرِمِينَ
12:110.en: [They continued] until, when the messengers despaired and were certain that they had been denied, there came to them Our victory, and whoever We willed was saved. And Our punishment cannot be repelled from the people who are criminals

O9kv0iYkyBQ.title: Seerah Ep 26: Abu Talib's Stand and the Boycott of Banu Hashim
O9kv0iYkyBQ.one_line: Abu Talib's warning to Quraysh over the assassination talk, and the three-year boycott of Banu Hashim as a lesson in principle and perseverance.
O9kv0iYkyBQ.summary: When talk of killing the Prophet surfaces in year seven, Abu Talib walks into Dar an-Nadwah with young men of Banu Hashim carrying hidden iron bars and warns the nobles off. He draws two lessons: communities need both the passion of youth and the wisdom of elders, and wisdom means knowing when to take a stand; the Prophet ignored insults, but open talk of murder in a place of law crossed the line, just as leaders who speak hatred today must never be tolerated. Humiliated, Quraysh impose the boycott. He describes the siege in the valley, Abu Lahab gloating and outbidding merchants, starvation to the point of eating leaves and an old piece of hide, and the striking fact that Muslims and non-Muslims of the clan endured together and none left, because the believers' ethics made them worth defending. He tells the story of Hisham ibn Amr smuggling food by camel, and of Khadijah staying when she was free to leave. He insists our role is different and easier: learn, stand out as a Muslim, spread knowledge, and persevere. The boycott taught the value of righteousness, and it ends with Amr ibn Abasah and the Prophet remembering his name years later.

outline.heading: Year seven in Mecca
outline.gist: Placing the coming events after the return of some emigrants from Abyssinia.

outline.heading: Talk of assassination reaches Abu Talib
outline.gist: For the first time the nobles speak of killing the Prophet, who faced nine plots yet never kept guards.

outline.heading: Abu Talib arms the young men of Banu Hashim
outline.gist: Hidden iron bars, not swords, and a planned signal.

outline.heading: Abu Talib confronts Dar an-Nadwah
outline.gist: Each noble finds a young man behind him; touch Muhammad and both sides will fight to the last.

outline.heading: Passion of the youth, wisdom of the elders
outline.gist: Progress needs both; youth alone make costly mistakes and elders alone change nothing.

outline.heading: Knowing when to take a stand
outline.gist: The Prophet did not react to insults and filth, but murder discussed in a place of law demanded a response; the caricatures raise the same question today.

outline.heading: Never tolerate leaders who speak hatred
outline.gist: Whether a principal, a CEO or a head of state, hatred toward any group must be opposed as a matter of principle.

outline.heading: The valley of Banu Hashim
outline.gist: How Meccan clans lived between mountains, poor in the valley and rich on the slopes.

outline.heading: The Prophet moved into the shi'b and the pact in the Ka'bah
outline.gist: No trade, no marriage, no entry or exit, signed in blood and hung in the Ka'bah.

outline.heading: The siege begins
outline.gist: Guards on both sides; everyone moves down into one dense neighbourhood, not knowing when it will end.

outline.heading: Non-Muslim relatives stand in solidarity
outline.gist: Most inside were not Muslim, yet they joined on principle against killing a man for his belief.

outline.heading: Abu Lahab's I told you so
outline.gist: Rubbing in a mistake is self-serving; give advice for Allah and leave it.

outline.heading: Abu Lahab outbids the merchants
outline.gist: He paid double so no one would sell to the besieged.

outline.heading: Why no one left: ethics worth defending
outline.gist: Not a single person left; non-Muslims stay with you only when your conduct is special.

outline.heading: The boycott was real, then and now
outline.gist: Fathers begged merchants for food for their children, as people still do in parts of the world today.

outline.heading: Eating leaves and holding to principle
outline.gist: Starvation to the point of eating like livestock, yet integrity would not be strong-armed.

outline.heading: How many of us would hold out?
outline.gist: One word of disowning him would have set them free; the weakness it caused later killed some of them.

outline.heading: Khadijah stays though free to leave
outline.gist: She never left his side and paid for it with her health and life.

outline.heading: The piece of camel hide
outline.gist: A companion cleaned and cooked an old hide and lived on it for three days; images of starved prisoners convey that pain.

outline.heading: Our role is different and easier
outline.gist: Our job is to educate ourselves, speak truth and stand out as Muslims at school; that is our perseverance.

outline.heading: Anas: love them and be with them
outline.gist: Anas loved the Prophet, Abu Bakr and Umar though he did not do what they did; he served by teaching until he died.

outline.heading: No miracles during the boycott
outline.gist: No food from the sky, and the companions never asked for it.

outline.heading: What Bilal hid under his arm
outline.gist: For thirty days the Prophet and Bilal ate only what Bilal could smuggle past the guards.

outline.heading: Hisham ibn Amr's camel
outline.gist: A non-Muslim noble trained his camel to carry food into the valley and was beaten each time he was caught.

outline.heading: Hatred can blind you
outline.gist: They nearly killed a man for feeding his relatives until someone stopped them.

outline.heading: Hisham's eventual Islam
outline.gist: Scholars link his guidance to that moment of truth.

outline.heading: Muslims and non-Muslims in harmony
outline.gist: No one told their non-Muslim defenders they were doomed; principle and ethics matter more than labels.

outline.heading: Why three years of nothing?
outline.gist: Numbers fell and da'wah stopped; earlier prophets were also denied and patient until victory came.

outline.heading: Righteousness is never obtained easily
outline.gist: It is the most valuable thing, and we must prove worthy of it.

outline.heading: Do your job and leave the outcome to Allah
outline.gist: No miracle will force belief; even prophets nearly despaired before help came.

outline.heading: What the boycott produced
outline.gist: Those who held firm in the valley stood by Islam until they died.

outline.heading: The Hajj respite
outline.gist: Only during the days of Hajj could the Prophet leave and pray at the Ka'bah.

outline.heading: Amr ibn Abasah meets the Prophet
outline.gist: A merchant accepts Islam, is told to return when the Prophet prevails, and walks away backwards to keep looking at him.

outline.heading: He remembered his name
outline.gist: Years later the Prophet greets Amr by name; caring hearts remember people, so work on remembering names.

43:9.ar: وَلَئِن سَأَلۡتَهُم مَّنۡ خَلَقَ ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلۡأَرۡضَ لَيَقُولُنَّ خَلَقَهُنَّ ٱلۡعَزِيزُ ٱلۡعَلِيمُ
43:9.en: And if you should ask them, "Who has created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Exalted in Might, the Knowing

43:10.ar: ٱلَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ ٱلۡأَرۡضَ مَهۡدࣰ ا وَجَعَلَ لَكُمۡ فِيهَا سُبُلࣰ ا لَّعَلَّكُمۡ تَهۡتَدُونَ
43:10.en: [The one] who has made for you the earth a bed and made for you upon it roads that you might be guided

43:11.ar: وَٱلَّذِي نَزَّلَ مِنَ ٱلسَّمَآءِ مَآءَۢ بِقَدَرࣲ فَأَنشَرۡنَا بِهِۦ بَلۡدَةࣰ مَّيۡتࣰ اۚ كَذَٰلِكَ تُخۡرَجُونَ
43:11.en: And who sends down rain from the sky in measured amounts, and We revive thereby a dead land - thus will you be brought forth

43:12.ar: وَٱلَّذِي خَلَقَ ٱلۡأَزۡوَٰجَ كُلَّهَا وَجَعَلَ لَكُم مِّنَ ٱلۡفُلۡكِ وَٱلۡأَنۡعَٰمِ مَا تَرۡكَبُونَ
43:12.en: And who created the species, all of them, and has made for you of ships and animals those which you mount

43:13.ar: لِتَسۡتَوُۥاْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِۦ ثُمَّ تَذۡكُرُواْ نِعۡمَةَ رَبِّكُمۡ إِذَا ٱسۡتَوَيۡتُمۡ عَلَيۡهِ وَتَقُولُواْ سُبۡحَٰنَ ٱلَّذِي سَخَّرَ لَنَا هَٰذَا وَمَا كُنَّا لَهُۥ مُقۡرِنِينَ
43:13.en: That you may settle yourselves upon their backs and then remember the favor of your Lord when you have settled upon them and say. "Exalted is He who has subjected this to us, and we could not have [otherwise] subdued it

43:14.en: And indeed we, to our Lord, will [surely] return

43:15.ar: وَجَعَلُواْ لَهُۥ مِنۡ عِبَادِهِۦ جُزۡءًاۚ إِنَّ ٱلۡإِنسَٰنَ لَكَفُورࣱ مُّبِينٌ
43:15.en: But they have attributed to Him from His servants a portion. Indeed, man is clearly ungrateful

43:16.ar: أَمِ ٱتَّخَذَ مِمَّا يَخۡلُقُ بَنَاتࣲ وَأَصۡفَىٰكُم بِٱلۡبَنِينَ
43:16.en: Or has He taken, out of what He has created, daughters and chosen you for [having] sons

43:17.ar: وَإِذَا بُشِّرَ أَحَدُهُم بِمَا ضَرَبَ لِلرَّحۡمَٰنِ مَثَلࣰ ا ظَلَّ وَجۡهُهُۥ مُسۡوَدࣰّ ا وَهُوَ كَظِيمٌ
43:17.en: And when one of them is given good tidings of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful in comparison, his face becomes dark, and he suppresses grief

43:18.ar: أَوَمَن يُنَشَّؤُاْ فِي ٱلۡحِلۡيَةِ وَهُوَ فِي ٱلۡخِصَامِ غَيۡرُ مُبِينࣲ‏
43:18.en: So is one brought up in ornaments while being during conflict unevident [attributed to Allah]

43:19.ar: وَجَعَلُواْ ٱلۡمَلَٰٓئِكَةَ ٱلَّذِينَ هُمۡ عِبَٰدُ ٱلرَّحۡمَٰنِ إِنَٰثًاۚ أَشَهِدُواْ خَلۡقَهُمۡۚ سَتُكۡتَبُ شَهَٰدَتُهُمۡ وَيُسۡـَٔلُونَ
43:19.en: And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned
